answer.decision: Adopt continuous transaction-log backups plus weekly full backups, retain recoverable month-end states for 12 months, tier older backups to cold storage, and test restores regularly.
answer.action: Configure database log backups at intervals of 15 minutes or less; create weekly full backups; preserve the full-and-log chains needed to recover each month-end for 12 months; move older eligible backups to cold storage; monitor storage savings; and run quarterly restore drills validating both the 15-minute RPO and two-hour RTO.
reasons: Continuous log backups can satisfy the database RPO while weekly fulls provide practical restore bases.
The prior weekly-full-plus-logs restore completed in 76 minutes; even adding the maximum 20-minute cold-tier delay gives 96 minutes, within the two-hour RTO.
Compliance requires 12-month month-end recoverability, not daily full backup images.
Daily full database backups generate 72 percent of current backup cost, so replacing most of them and tiering older data should comfortably exceed the required 35 percent reduction.
Customer documents already have independent versioning and lifecycle tiering, making the database policy the principal remaining savings opportunity.
assumptions: Transaction logs will be captured and durably stored at least every 15 minutes without gaps.
Cold-tier retrieval delay can be added to the observed 76-minute restore time without other material delays.
Weekly fulls and retained log chains are designed so every required month-end state remains recoverable for 12 months.
Backup data sizes, compression, and storage prices remain sufficiently similar to the supplied evidence for the projected savings to hold.
risks: A missing or corrupt transaction-log segment could break point-in-time recovery and month-end recoverability.
Cold-tier congestion or restore processing variance could reduce the 24-minute margin under the RTO.
Log growth, full-backup growth, retrieval charges, or minimum-storage fees could reduce realized savings.
Poor retention-chain management could delete logs or full backups still required for compliance.
Restore success shown by one drill may not represent larger future datasets, so recurring tests and alerting are essential.

citations.claim: Daily full database backups account for 72 percent of current backup storage cost.
Point-in-time recovery logs average 6 percent of a daily full backup's storage per day.
Compliance requires 12-month recoverability of month-end records but does not require daily full images.
A weekly-full-plus-logs restore completed in 76 minutes.
Cold storage costs 68 percent less per GB and can add up to 20 minutes of retrieval delay.
Document objects already use versioning and lifecycle tiering, leaving database backups as the dominant cost lever.
